screens.heading: The problem: messy tables
screens.body:
Imagine one giant table holding orders, customers, and products all mixed together. Customer names repeat on every order row. That's redundant — and redundancy breeds bugs.

If a customer changes their phone number, you must update ten rows. Miss one, and your data contradicts itself. These are called update anomalies.

check.question: Storing a customer's phone on every order row risks…
options: Update anomalies — changing it in one place but not another

screens.heading: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
screens.body:
First normal form says: every cell holds one single value — atomic, indivisible. No lists, no comma-separated phone numbers in one cell.

It also bans repeating groups: instead of phone1, phone2, phone3 columns, use a separate table (or rows). One fact per cell, one kind of fact per table.
screens.keyPoint: One value per cell. No lists, no repeating columns.

check.question: Which violates 1NF?
options: A separate Phones table with one number per row

screens.heading: 2NF: the whole key, nothing but the key
screens.body:
Second normal form builds on 1NF: every non-key column must depend on the whole primary key — not just part of it.

If a table's key is (order_id, product_id) but product_name depends only on product_id, that's a partial dependency. Move product_name into a Products table keyed by product_id.
screens.keyPoint: No column may depend on only part of the key.

check.question: In an OrderItems table keyed by (order_id, product_id), product_name depends only on product_id. This violates…

screens.heading: 3NF: no transitive dependencies
screens.body:
Third normal form: no non-key column may depend on another non-key column. Dependencies must go straight to the key — no middlemen.

If customer_id → city, and city → tax_rate, then tax_rate depends transitively on customer_id through city. Move (city, tax_rate) into its own table.
screens.keyPoint: Non-key columns can't depend on other non-key columns.

check.question: A table has customer_id → city → tax_rate. To reach 3NF you…
options: Move city and tax_rate into their own table

screens.heading: The ladder: 1NF → 2NF → 3NF
screens.body:
Each normal form includes the ones below it: 3NF implies 2NF implies 1NF. You climb the ladder one rung at a time.

In practice, most working databases land at 3NF. It kills the common anomalies without splitting tables into confetti. Know the ladder; aim for the third rung.

screens.heading: When to break the rules: denormalization
screens.body:
Normalization optimizes for correct writes; sometimes reads matter more. A report that joins six tables a thousand times a day might deserve a pre-computed column.

That's denormalization: deliberately reintroducing redundancy for speed. It's a trade-off, not a failure — you accept trickier writes for faster reads.

check.question: Denormalization is…
options: Deliberate redundancy traded for faster reads

screens.heading: Normalization in practice
screens.body:
Take an Orders table with customer_name and customer_phone on every row. Step one: pull customers into their own table with a customer_id key — the repeated data vanishes.

Orders keeps just customer_id as a foreign key. Update a phone number once, and every order instantly reflects it. That's the whole payoff in one move.
screens.keyPoint: Split repeating groups into their own tables.

code.snippet:
-- before: Orders(order_id, customer_name, customer_phone, ...)
-- after:
CREATE TABLE Customers (
    customer_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT,
    phone TEXT
);

check.question: After splitting customers out of Orders, a phone change needs…
options: One update in the Customers table
